tool_args.old_string: \paragraph{SDF integration pathways.} SDF-based geometric supervision can enter VLA policies through three mechanisms: (a)~\emph{training-time auxiliary loss} on the EE trajectory (tested here); (b)~\emph{constrained optimization}, where SafeVLA~\citep{zhang2025safevla} embeds safety constraints via Lagrangian optimization; and (c)~\emph{runtime filtering}, where VLSA~\citep{hu2025vlsa} applies control barrier functions at inference. Our negative finding is specific to pathway~(a) and does not imply limitations for~(b) or~(c).
tool_args.new_string: \paragraph{SDF integration pathways.} SDF-based geometric supervision can enter VLA policies through three mechanisms: (a)~\emph{training-time auxiliary loss} on the EE trajectory (tested here); (b)~\emph{constrained optimization}, where SafeVLA~\citep{zhang2025safevla} embeds safety constraints via Lagrangian optimization; and (c)~\emph{runtime filtering}, where VLSA~\citep{hu2025vlsa} applies control barrier functions at inference. These pathways differ in where geometric information acts. Pathway~(a) shapes learned representations but provides gradients only at the supervised point---here, the EE---leaving intermediate links unmonitored. Pathways~(b) and~(c) can in principle query full-body geometry at optimization or inference time, sidestepping the single-point bottleneck that our results identify as the binding constraint. Our negative finding is specific to pathway~(a) and does not imply limitations for~(b) or~(c).

Our work reveals that restricting SDF supervision to a single kinematic point (the EE) within a learned policy does not transfer these full-body benefits.

\paragraph{Vision-Language-Action Models.}
VLA models combine pretrained vision-language backbones with action prediction for generalist manipulation~\cite{brohan2023rt2,black2024pi0,chi2023diffusionpolicy,kim2024openvla}. Recent work enhances spatial reasoning through auxiliary 3D supervision~\cite{li2025spatialforcing,li2025qdepth,depthvla2025}, but safety considerations remain largely absent: most VLAs train on collision-free demonstrations and evaluate task success alone, with no mechanism to distinguish genuine avoidance from incidental collision-free trajectories.
tool_args.new_string:
\paragraph{Vision-Language-Action Models.}
VLA models combine pretrained vision-language backbones with action prediction for generalist manipulation~\cite{brohan2023rt2,black2024pi0,chi2023diffusionpolicy,kim2024openvla}. Recent work enhances spatial reasoning through auxiliary 3D supervision~\cite{li2025spatialforcing,li2025qdepth,depthvla2025}, but these methods improve scene understanding and grasping precision without incorporating collision constraints; the auxiliary depth or spatial predictions serve perception rather than safety. Most VLAs train on collision-free demonstrations and evaluate task success alone, with no mechanism to distinguish genuine avoidance from incidental collision-free trajectories. Whether geometric supervision can bridge this gap---teaching a policy to actively avoid obstacles rather than merely perceive them---is the question our work addresses.

tool_args.old_string: Common to all is that safety is imposed externally. This work tests whether auxiliary SDF supervision can produce intrinsic collision awareness.
tool_args.new_string: Common to all is that safety is imposed extrinsically---as a constraint or filter applied to an otherwise safety-unaware policy. Extrinsic approaches add inference-time overhead and require access to collision geometry at deployment. A key open question is whether safety can instead be learned intrinsically, embedded in the policy's representations during training, so that the policy avoids collisions without a runtime shield. This work tests whether auxiliary SDF supervision can produce such intrinsic collision awareness.

tool_args.old_string: We propose dfCAR (\S\ref{sec:dfcar}) to detect this contamination.
tool_args.new_string: More broadly, any binary safety metric faces a base-rate problem: when most episodes are collision-free---either genuinely or through inaction---the metric offers limited discriminative power, paralleling class-imbalance vulnerabilities where a trivial predictor achieves high accuracy on skewed data~\cite{gururangan2018annotation}. We propose dfCAR (\S\ref{sec:dfcar}) to address this confound by conditioning on active behavior, restricting the evaluation to episodes where the robot meaningfully engages with the task environment.

1	\section{The Action-Collapsed Safety Problem}\label{sec:fake_safety}
2	
3	Standard CAR assumes that collision-free episodes reflect deliberate avoidance. This assumption is systematically violated: in every Pi0 configuration tested, over 99\% of collision-free episodes are action-collapse artifacts (Table~\ref{tab:fake_safety}).\footnote{Pi0-family values report obstacle displacement from the original protocol; Pi0.5 reports EE displacement from the rotation-corrected protocol (\S\ref{sec:dfcar}). Sub-millimeter displacement indicates action collapse in both cases.} Applying dfCAR collapses all three to ${\approx}$\,0\%. Pi0+A1 achieves the \emph{highest} raw CAR (91.5\%) because more complete action collapse (from a parameter-name mismatch preventing LoRA loading; Table~\ref{tab:configurations}) yields greater CAR inflation. Pi0.5 validates the metric from the opposite direction: every safe episode exceeds 200\,mm displacement, and dfCAR equals raw CAR (28.5\%). The displacement distribution is sharply bimodal (Appendix~\ref{sec:appendix_displacement}), with a five-order-of-magnitude gap that makes $\tau_d$ robust.
